claims.text: In the Von Neumann model, a computer system has one memory holding both the program's instructions and its data, a single processor, and input, output and storage devices, connected by buses.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The stored program concept means a program's instructions are held in memory like its data, so a computer changes its task by loading a different program, with no change to its construction.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A register is a small, fast store inside the CPU; the Program Counter (PC) is a special purpose register holding the memory address of the instruction that will be fetched next.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The Memory Address Register (MAR) holds the address of the memory location being accessed, and the Memory Data Register (MDR) holds the data or instruction being read from or written to memory.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The Current Instruction Register (CIR) holds the instruction currently being executed, and the Accumulator (ACC) is the register where the ALU's working results are held.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The Index Register (IX) holds a base address used with indexed addressing, and the Status Register holds flags about the last operation, such as whether the result was zero, negative or caused overflow.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A general purpose register is one a program may use for its own working values, whereas a special purpose register has one fixed role, such as the PC's or the MAR's.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU) performs the arithmetic and logic operations of the program, such as addition, subtraction and comparisons, placing its result in the accumulator and setting the status flags.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The Control Unit (CU) is one part of the CPU: it decodes the instruction in the CIR and sends control signals to the other components to carry it out.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The system clock generates regular timing pulses that synchronise the CPU's steps, so a higher clock speed means more instruction stages complete per second.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The data bus carries the actual data and instructions between components, the address bus carries memory addresses, and the control bus carries control and timing signals such as read and write.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A wider address bus can address more memory, and a wider data bus moves more bits per transfer, so both bus widths contribute to the computer's performance.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A computer system's performance depends on the processor type, the number of cores, the clock speed, the bus widths and the cache memory available.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: More cores let a computer run instructions from separate programs at the same time, so several programs progress together, though a single program does not speed up unless it is written to use them.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Cache memory sits between the processor and main memory and holds a copy of the instructions and data the processor is most likely to need next, which it reaches faster than a main-memory fetch.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A port is a physical connection through which a peripheral device is attached to the computer.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: USB connects a wide range of peripherals, such as keyboards, storage devices and printers; HDMI carries digital video and audio to a display, whereas VGA carries analogue video signals only.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In the fetch stage, the PC's address is copied to the MAR, the PC is incremented, the instruction at the address held in the MAR is read into the MDR, and the MDR's contents are copied to the CIR.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In the decode stage the control unit interprets the instruction in the CIR and sends control signals to prepare what it needs; in the execute stage the instruction is carried out, an arithmetic result going to the accumulator.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: During the fetch of every instruction the processor checks for interrupts, and an enabled interrupt is serviced before the next instruction is fetched.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An interrupt is a signal that makes the processor pause its current program, run an interrupt service routine (ISR) for that cause, and then resume the interrupted program.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Causes of interrupts include input arriving, a timer expiring, a hardware fault and a program error; each cause has its own interrupt service routine, and the processor checks the interrupt's priority before servicing it, because some events must be answered at once.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).
